phenomena.title: Recursion & fractals
phenomena.summary: Rules repeated across scales: exact self-similarity, branching models, rough edges, nested forms, and recursive worlds.

topics.title: When equal circles meet
topics.summary: Move two equal circles and watch separation, tangency, lens, and intersection points emerge from one changing distance.

topics.title: The triangle hidden in two circles
topics.summary: When each equal circle passes through the other's center, either intersection joins the centers to make three equal sides.

topics.title: Euclid begins with this move
topics.summary: Book I, Proposition 1 of the Elements constructs an equilateral triangle from a segment using two equal-radius circles.

topics.title: Three triangles, one charged absence
topics.summary: An essay on how meaning was added to three triangles, by masons, a clan, a publisher, and its players — with the popular lineage marked as the folklore it is.

topics.title: Seven ways to fall in fours
topics.summary: An essay on a game with no content: seven counted shapes, and a nation, a song, and a sensation that were all added to them later by people who can be named.

topics.title: The two moves that keep a shape
topics.summary: Flip a figure across a line or turn it about a point: the moves that change nothing measurable, collected, become the figure's symmetry group.

topics.title: Seven ways down an endless strip
topics.summary: Repeat a motif along one direction, add mirrors, glides, and half-turns in any consistent mix, and every possible strip pattern lands in one of exactly seven families.

topics.title: Seventeen patterns exhaust the plane
topics.summary: A pattern repeating in two independent directions has one of exactly seventeen symmetry groups—no eighteenth exists. The lab draws a labeled subset; the count of seventeen rests on the cited literature.

topics.title: Counting symmetries at the Alhambra
topics.summary: How many of the seventeen wallpaper groups decorate the Alhambra? Müller counted fewer than all of them in 1944; later authors argue for all seventeen. The disagreement—over what counts as a pattern—is the topic.

relationships.summary: Each intersection is one radius from both centers.
Euclid's first proposition records this two-circle construction.
The game emblem can be analyzed as three congruent triangles around a central triangular absence; resemblance does not establish historical influence.
Both expose one replacement rule returning at smaller scales, although their geometry and limits differ.
Repeated smaller curls invite comparison with self-similarity; no historical influence or intent is claimed.
Branching and terrain subdivision repeatedly transform earlier structure into finer detail.
The exact Koch replacement and a rough terrain model both demonstrate detail introduced across scales; they are not the same algorithm.
The equilateral triangle is the smallest rich example: three mirrors and three rotations close into one six-element symmetry group.
A single row of star-and-cross tiles repeats along one direction, so its border reads as a frieze pattern and lands in one of the seven families.
Each regular tiling repeats in two independent directions, so it carries one of the seventeen wallpaper groups; the crystallographic restriction bounds the rotations both topics share.
Wallpaper groups require two independent translations; a Penrose tiling has none, so the seventeen-way classification does not apply to it—order without a period escapes the list.
Which of the seventeen groups the Alhambra's ornament realizes remains contested; the mathematics is settled, the attribution is not.

claims.text: Every point on a circle is the radius-distance from its center.
If equal-radius circles have centers one radius apart, an intersection and the two centers form a triangle whose three sides are all one radius.
Book I, Proposition 1 of Euclid's Elements constructs an equilateral triangle on a given segment with two circles centered at its endpoints.
Nintendo's official Zelda site describes the Triforce as a magical object made of three golden triangles.
Nintendo's official history dates the first Legend of Zelda release to 21 February 1986 on the Family Computer Disk System.
Three congruent upward equilateral triangles can be arranged into a larger triangular composition around a congruent downward central space.
Repeating the same two-branch rule with a constant length ratio produces exact self-similarity across its discrete levels.
IBM's institutional history credits Benoît Mandelbrot with coining the term fractal and using computer graphics to reveal repeated structure across scales.
Helge von Koch's 1904 publication described a continuous curve without tangents obtained through an elementary geometric construction.
Replacing every segment with four segments one third as long gives 4 to the power n segments and total length multiplied by 4 over 3 at each iteration.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art identifies Hokusai's Under the Wave off Kanagawa as a Japanese woodblock print from the Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji series, made about 1830–32.
The original diagram compares successively smaller curls with visual echoes in the wave; it does not claim Hokusai intended or knew modern fractal geometry.
David Fox's creator-owned project page reproduces the game credits naming Loren Carpenter for 3-D fractal landscape image generation and co-creation of the concept.
MobyGames records 1985 releases of Rescue on Fractalus! for Atari 8-bit, Apple II, and Commodore 64.
The interactive profile uses deterministic midpoint subdivision to demonstrate recursive terrain detail; it is not a reproduction of the historical game algorithm.
For a tiling by one regular polygon at every vertex, its interior angle must divide 360 degrees; only the equilateral triangle, square, and regular hexagon satisfy this condition.
The hexagonal arrangement of equal circles covers a fraction pi divided by square root of 12, approximately 0.9069, of the plane.
Kepler's 1611 pamphlet on the six-cornered snowflake examined hexagonal form and packing questions.

The Metropolitan Museum records this eight-pointed star-shaped stonepaste tile as made in Kashan, Iran, in the thirteenth century, and notes that its current star-and-cross panel combines tiles from differing original contexts.
The Star and Cross pattern can be constructed from eight-pointed {8/2} regular star polygons on a square grid; their interstitial spaces form the cross tiles.
Penrose's patent describes two quadrilateral tile types with matching constraints whose plane assemblies are necessarily non-repetitive and based on fivefold symmetry.
The National Gallery of Art records M. C. Escher's Regular Division of the Plane I as a 1957 woodcut.
The official Tetris account states that Pajitnov's 1984 design used seven geometric pieces, each made from four squares, moved and rotated in a rectangular Matrix to complete rows.
There are eleven convex uniform tilings of the Euclidean plane by regular polygons: three regular and eight semiregular vertex-transitive tilings.

For regular polygons around a vertex, an angle sum below, equal to, or above 360 degrees corresponds locally to positive, zero, or negative curvature; local closure alone does not prove global extendability.
Georges Voronoi published his second memoir on continuous parameters and primitive parallelohedra in 1908.
Five-, eight-, ten-, and twelve-fold rotations cannot preserve a two-dimensional periodic lattice; crystallographic planar rotation orders are limited to one, two, three, four, and six.
Penrose tilings have a golden-ratio hierarchical structure; under repeated rhomb substitution the thick-to-thin tile frequency approaches the golden ratio.
The pentagrid method of de Bruijn constructs Penrose rhomb tilings by dualizing five families of parallel lines; the displayed finite patch uses this method.
A reflection or a rotation of the plane is an isometry: a map that preserves the distance between every pair of points.
The symmetry-preserving operations of a figure—its rotations and reflections—form a group under composition.
There are exactly seven frieze groups classifying the symmetry types of patterns that repeat along a single direction.
Up to equivalence there are exactly seventeen wallpaper groups: the plane symmetry groups of patterns that repeat in two independent directions.

The classification of the crystallographic groups, including the seventeen planar groups, was achieved at the end of the nineteenth century by E. S. Fedorov, with A. Schoenflies arriving slightly later.
George Pólya added to the understanding of the seventeen plane crystallographic groups in 1924 by illustrating each of them.
The lab's visual presents a labeled subset of the seventeen wallpaper groups; the count of seventeen rests on the cited literature, not on the display.
Grünbaum's 2006 review reports that Edith Müller's 1944 group-theoretic study of the Alhambra's ornament documented fewer than all seventeen wallpaper groups there.

Published counts of wallpaper groups present in the Alhambra range from Müller's fewer-than-seventeen to later claims of all seventeen; the answer depends on which ornaments, colourings, and interlacings are admitted as patterns, and Grünbaum's 2006 review treats the question as unsettled.

The arrangement is the first step of the Sierpiński gasket: begin with an equilateral triangle, remove an inverted triangle of half the side length, and repeat without end. Sierpiński introduced the construction in 1915.

Compositions recognizable as Sierpiński triangles, iterated to at least three levels, are set into the stone floors of medieval Roman churches, centuries before the mathematics was described. The paper identifies the compositions; it does not claim the makers understood them as self-similar.
The mitsuuroko, three scales arranged as three triangles in a triangle, is the mon of the Hōjō clan, regents of the Kamakura shogunate between 1203 and 1333.

In the legend carried by the Taiheiki tradition and retold by Enoshima Shrine, Hōjō Tokimasa kept a vigil in the Enoshima caves, the goddess Benzaiten appeared and foretold his line's rule, and three dragon scales were left behind, which he took as his banner. This is recorded as a legend, not as an event.

That the Hōjō mon inspired the Triforce is widely repeated. No statement from Nintendo or its designers documenting that lineage was located in this review. The visual resemblance is plain; the causal link is undocumented.
The item called the Bible in the Japanese original became the Book of Magic in the English localization of the first Legend of Zelda.

Read together, these layers suggest that the significance of this figure was added to it repeatedly, by masons, by a clan, by a publisher's fiction, by a localization team, and by players inventing a lineage. This is the essay's argument and not a finding.

There are exactly seven one-sided tetrominoes — shapes of four squares joined edge to edge, counted so that rotations are the same shape but mirror images are not. Counting mirror images as the same shape gives five.
A falling piece can be rotated but never flipped over, so the two chiral pairs, S with Z and J with L, are different pieces in play. That rule is what makes the count seven rather than five.

Alexey Pajitnov designed Tetris in 1984 while working at the Dorodnicyn Computing Centre of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR in Moscow. It was written for the Elektronika 60 and ported to the IBM PC by Vadim Gerasimov.
The name comes from the Greek tetra, four: each of the seven pieces is made of four squares.

The Western Spectrum HoloByte release presented the game through Russian imagery that the original did not contain: Saint Basil's Cathedral, the title in Russian lettering with a sickle worked into the last character, an outline of the USSR in the manual, the phrase 'The Soviet Challenge', and the advertising line 'The Cold War is Over. Almost…'

The Game Boy 'Type A' theme is Korobeiniki, a Russian folk song adapted from Nikolay Nekrasov's 1861 poem about a peddler bargaining with a girl in a field. Hirokazu Tanaka arranged it for Nintendo's 1989 release; earlier commercial versions did not carry it.

In a 2000 study in Science, people who played Tetris reported intrusive images of falling pieces at sleep onset. Three amnesic patients with extensive bilateral medial temporal lobe damage reported the same imagery while being unable to recall having played, which indicates the imagery does not depend on declarative memory.

The game contains a counted set of shapes and one rule. Everything else it is felt to mean — a nation, a era, a piece of music, a sensation that outlasts the session — was added afterwards by people who can be named. This is the essay's argument and not a finding.
